name: Wardrobe capsule / minimalist wardrobe

lead: A capsule wardrobe is a small collection of staple clothes in coordinating colors that combine into many outfits, so you look coordinated without much effort. The better-dressed look shows on the day it is worn.

The term appeared in American publications in the 1940s, was revived in the 1970s by London boutique owner Susie Faux, and was popularized by Donna Karan in 1985 with her 7 Easy Pieces collection. No studies have tested its effect on attractiveness, and coverage of the concept is mostly fashion media and blogs.

paras: People pick a limited palette and a set of basics, such as jeans, a blazer and a coat, make sure each piece fits well, and mix them in different combinations. Many clear out pieces that do not combine with the rest.
No harms are documented. Proponents say it is budget-friendly, though quality basics can cost more per piece.

angle.text: A small set of well-fitting, interchangeable staples makes every outfit look coordinated, and the put-together look is visible the day you wear it. It is a long-standing fashion idea rather than something tested in attractiveness studies.

lead: A capsule wardrobe is a small collection of clothes that can be combined into many outfits, usually built from staple items in coordinating colours [1]. In looksmaxxing and style communities it is discussed as a way to dress well consistently: a few well-fitting, interchangeable basics mean every outfit works, the owner always has something suitable to wear, and spending goes on fit and quality rather than volume.

The term appeared in American publications in the 1940s for small groups of garments that harmonised in colour and line, and was revived in the 1970s by London boutique owner Susie Faux for a set of essentials that would not go out of fashion, supplemented by seasonal pieces. Donna Karan popularised the idea in 1985 with her 7 Easy Pieces collection of interchangeable workwear [1].
Stylist Gok Wan has argued that the approach helps people look good on a small budget, especially in a recession [1].

paras: The collection is built from key items in coordinating colours so that few garments cover a range of occasions [1]. Wikipedia gives example lists, with a women's version including a trench coat, jeans, a white shirt, a black blazer, a dress and flats, and a men's version including a suit, jeans, a coat, T-shirts, a blazer and a watch [1]. Items that do not go out of fashion can be worn across seasons and updated with seasonal pieces [1].
The Oxford English Dictionary dates the American sense of capsule as small and compact to 1938, and the term was used in the 1940s for small groups of garments harmonising in colour and line [1].
Susie Faux, owner of the Wardrobe boutique in London, revived the term in the 1970s [1]. Donna Karan's 7 Easy Pieces, in 1985, showed interchangeable workwear for working women [1].

UK newspapers and magazines such as Marie Claire and Elle ran features on the concept, and television shows including What Not to Wear (BBC, 2001 to 2007) and Gok's Fashion Fix (Channel 4, from 2008) helped popularise it [1]. Wikipedia's related-topics list includes simple living and normcore [1].
No studies found on the effect of a capsule wardrobe on perceived attractiveness.

timeline.event: Oxford English Dictionary dates the American use of capsule as small and compact.[1]
Susie Faux revives the term capsule wardrobe in London.[1]
Gok's Fashion Fix begins on Channel 4.[1]
